blocks.title: Starch changes
blocks.md: In cold water starch granules do not dissolve. On heating in water (roughly 60 to 80 degrees Celsius, depending on the starch) they absorb water and swell, and amylose leaches out: **gelatinisation**, which thickens sauces and porridge (pap). On cooling and standing, starch chains re-associate: **retrogradation** (staling of bread, firming of cold fufu, syneresis in gels). Heating dry starch strongly produces **dextrins** (browning of toast).

blocks.title: Sugar reactions
blocks.md: **Hydrolysis** of sucrose (by acid or the enzyme invertase) gives equal amounts of glucose and fructose: **invert sugar**, sweeter than sucrose and more soluble, used in jam and confectionery. **Caramelisation**: sucrose heated strongly (above about 160 degrees Celsius) decomposes and browns without amino acids. The **Maillard reaction**: **reducing sugars react with amino groups** of amino acids or proteins on heating, giving brown colours and flavours (crust of bread, roasted groundnuts, fried plantain). It lowers the availability of some amino acids (lysine).

blocks.caption: Three stages: intact granules in cold water, gelatinisation on heating and retrogradation on cooling.
blocks.alt: Flow of starch changes: intact, gelatinised, retrograded.

blocks.title: Sugar in food
blocks.md: Sugar sweetens, gives texture and bulk, retains moisture, and in high concentration (jam, syrup) lowers **water activity**, preserving food. Acrylamide, a compound of health concern, can form in some starchy foods cooked at very high temperatures (frying, baking); avoid over-browning.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Caramelisation needs no protein; Maillard needs a reducing sugar and an amino group.
- Gelatinisation is not the same as dissolving.
- Retrogradation is the reverse of 'freshness', not of cooking.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Browning
blocks.statement: Name the process that browns (a) sugar heated alone, (b) a bread crust.
steps: (a) Sugar alone browns by caramelisation (no amino acids).
(b) The crust browns mainly by the Maillard reaction between reducing sugars and amino acids.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Invert sugar
blocks.statement: Equal amounts of which sugars form on hydrolysis of sucrose?
steps: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.
Hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond giving glucose and fructose.

blocks.title: Protein structure and denaturation
blocks.md: Proteins have **primary** (amino acid sequence), **secondary** (helix, sheet), **tertiary** (folded shape) and sometimes **quaternary** structure. **Denaturation** is unfolding by heat, acid, alkali, salt or whipping, losing the native shape without breaking peptide bonds. In food it causes **coagulation** (egg white sets at roughly 60 to 80 degrees Celsius), curdling of milk with acid, firming of meat. Over-heating squeezes out water and toughens protein.

blocks.title: Gels, foams and gluten
blocks.md: A **gel** forms when denatured protein chains form a network that traps water (gelatine, egg custard, yoghurt). A **foam** (whipped egg white) is gas trapped in a protein film. **Gluten** forms from wheat proteins (gliadin and glutenin) when flour is kneaded with water: an elastic network that traps gas in bread dough; it is not formed by maize or cassava flours.

items.text: Chains link up: gel, white solid (coagulation)

blocks.caption: Three stages of egg white: folded protein, unfolding on heating and coagulation into a solid.
blocks.alt: Flow: native protein, denaturation by heat, coagulation.

blocks.title: Lipid changes
blocks.md: **Rancidity**: **hydrolytic** (lipase or water releases free fatty acids, a soapy taste) and **oxidative** (oxygen attacks double bonds, giving off-flavours; faster with heat, light, metal ions and more unsaturation). **Antioxidants** slow oxidation. **Hydrogenation** adds hydrogen to double bonds, making oils more solid and stable; partial hydrogenation can create **trans** fatty acids. An **emulsion** mixes oil and water with an **emulsifier** (lecithin in egg yolk keeps mayonnaise stable). The **smoke point** is the temperature at which a fat starts to smoke and break down; repeated heating lowers it and forms harmful products.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Denaturation does not break peptide bonds (digestion does).
- Hydrogenated does not automatically mean trans: complete hydrogenation gives saturated fat.
- Re-using frying oil many times is not recommended.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Mayonnaise
blocks.statement: Why does mayonnaise stay mixed although it is oil in a watery base?
steps: Egg yolk contains lecithin, an emulsifier.
It stabilises tiny oil droplets so they do not separate.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Fats on storage
blocks.statement: Why does groundnut oil stored in a clear bottle in the sun turn rancid faster?
steps: Light and heat speed up oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids.
Store in a cool, dark, tightly closed container.

blocks.title: Enzymes
blocks.md: **Enzymes** are protein catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering activation energy; each has an **active site** specific to its **substrate**. Activity depends on **temperature** (rate rises up to the optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures), **pH**, substrate and enzyme concentration, and inhibitors. Few enzymes survive above about 70 degrees Celsius.

blocks.title: Enzymic browning
blocks.md: Cut yam, banana, apple or avocado turns brown because **polyphenol oxidase** uses oxygen to convert phenolic compounds to brown pigments. Control: **blanching** (a short heat treatment that inactivates enzymes), **acid** (lemon juice lowers the pH), **excluding oxygen** (sealing, water), **cold** and **antioxidants** such as vitamin C.

blocks.caption: A bar chart showing relative enzyme activity rising to a maximum near 40 degrees and falling at higher temperatures.
blocks.alt: Bar chart showing enzyme rate low at 0 and 20 degrees, highest at 40, low at 60 and zero at 80 degrees Celsius.

blocks.title: Useful enzymes
blocks.md: **Amylase**: converts starch to sugars (malting, syrups). **Papain** (from pawpaw) and **bromelain** (from pineapple): proteases that tenderise meat. **Rennet** (chymosin): clots milk for cheese. **Pectinase**: clarifies fruit juice. **Invertase**: soft-centred sweets. **Lactase**: lactose-free milk. Natural enzymes also cause unwanted changes: ripening, softening and off-flavours.

blocks.title: Blanching
blocks.md: Vegetables are heated briefly (for example in boiling water for a minute or two) and cooled quickly before freezing or drying. This inactivates enzymes that would otherwise cause colour, texture and flavour changes during storage, and reduces surface microorganisms. Some water-soluble vitamins are lost, so keep blanching short.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Enzymes are not killed by freezing: they slow down and can resume on thawing.
- High temperature does not make enzymes 'tired' - it denatures them.
- Browning of cut fruit is not caused by microorganisms.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Browning
blocks.statement: Suggest two ways to stop sliced avocado browning at a party.
steps: Cover tightly to exclude air, and keep cool.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Tenderising
blocks.statement: Why can fresh pawpaw leaves or fruit tenderise tough meat?
steps: Papain breaks down connective-tissue proteins in the meat.
